prompt: Why did Hungary's central bank invent the milpengő and the b.-pengő in 1946?
options: To cut the number of zeros needed on banknotes
To pay war reparations in a separate currency
To replace gold coins that had been melted down
To give soldiers a currency of their own
correctAnswer: To cut the number of zeros needed on banknotes
explanation: A milpengő was a million pengő and a b.-pengő a million million. Even so, the record note still stood for 100 quintillion pengő.

prompt: In New France's card money, the suit mattered: a jack of hearts was worth more than a 3 of spades.
explanation: The face of the card meant nothing. Officials wrote a value on the plain back and signed it, and cards were cut to different shapes to tell the values apart.

prompt: After smoking bans hit US federal prisons around 2004, the usual currency became pouches of __________.
explanation: A pouch cost about $1 and few people wanted to eat it, which made it a handy stand-in for the dollar. Inmates may not hold cash.

prompt: Why were prices in New France rising by the early 1690s?
options: Many cards were never handed in, so the colony could keep spending with new ones
The cards were printed on gold leaf
Merchants refused to accept any coins
The King doubled every soldier's pay
correctAnswer: Many cards were never handed in, so the colony could keep spending with new ones
explanation: People found the cards useful as money, so they kept them rather than redeeming them. More money chasing the same goods pushes prices up, which is why the cards were finally redeemed at half value in 1717.

prompt: Match each money to where it circulated:

pairs.right: A US state prison studied in 2016

explanation: Money can be anything people trust others to accept. Card money and the pengő were official; macks and soups grew up on their own, where cash was banned.

prompt: What did Hanoi's 1902 rat bounty ask people to hand in as proof of a kill?
options: The rat's tail
The whole dead rat
The rat's head
A form signed by a neighbor
explanation: Tails were easy to count and store, but a rat could lose its tail and live. Soon officials were seeing tailless rats in the streets.

prompt: Historians have found the colonial records of the Delhi cobra bounty that gave the cobra effect its name.
explanation: There is little evidence the Delhi story happened; the term itself comes from Horst Siebert's 2001 book. The well-documented backfiring bounty is Hanoi's rat hunt of 1902.

prompt: Gneezy and Rustichini called their study of late parents at Haifa day-care centers "A Fine Is a __________."
explanation: A 10-shekel fine told parents exactly what lateness cost, and it was cheap. Late pickups nearly doubled and stayed high after the fine was dropped.

prompt: Lucas Davis found that Mexico City's Hoy No Circula did not improve air quality. What was a main reason?
options: Households acquired extra cars, many of them used and higher-emitting
The police did not enforce the ban
Most banned drivers switched to the subway
The ban applied only to taxis and buses
correctAnswer: Households acquired extra cars, many of them used and higher-emitting
explanation: A second car with a different final digit beats the ban every day. Davis also found no rise in subway or bus ridership, and pollution shifted toward weekends and nights.

prompt: Match each policy to the way people responded:

pairs.right: Cutting off tails and letting rats breed
Paying for lateness as if it were a service
Buying a second car with a different plate

explanation: Each rule rewarded or punished a measurable proxy, and people found the cheapest way to change the proxy rather than the thing the rule cared about.

prompt: What post did the Scottish gambler John Law take in France in January 1720?
options: Finance minister (controller-general)
Commander of the French army
Governor of Louisiana
Head of the Paris police
explanation: By then his company also collected France's taxes and ran its mints, so one man controlled both the money and the shares whose price it propped up.

prompt: Andrew Odlyzko argues that George Hudson's accounting fraud was the main cause of the Railway Mania's losses.
explanation: Hudson's frauds were real, but Odlyzko blames over-optimistic forecasts: the new lines cost more to build and earned less than promised, so even honest railways saw profits fall.

prompt: Collectors bought plastic lockets to protect a Beanie Baby's heart-shaped paper __________, even though it told owners to remove it before giving the toy to a child.
explanation: Collectors believed a perfect tag protected a Beanie's resale value, so the safety advice printed on it was ignored.

prompt: Which Ty Inc. practice did most to make some Beanie Babies scarce and expensive?
options: Retiring characters so they stopped being made
Selling them only in big chain stores
Heavy television advertising
Raising prices every month
correctAnswer: Retiring characters so they stopped being made
explanation: Retirement turned a cheap toy into a collectible. Once retirement announcements stopped producing spikes in demand in 1999, the bubble had nothing left to feed it.

prompt: Match each name to its place in a mania:

pairs.right: Paris street where Mississippi shares were traded
The Railway King, exposed for fraud in 1849
Magazine with a million paid copies a month
Minis handed out in McDonald's Happy Meals in 1997

explanation: Each mania had its own marketplace and its own heroes. In all three, buyers paid because they expected prices to keep rising, not because of what the shares or toys would earn.

prompt: Joel Waldfogel's surveys found that holiday gift-giving destroys roughly how much of the value of gifts?
options: Between 10 percent and a third
About 1 percent
About two thirds
None, because gifts are worth more than they cost
explanation: The loss is the gap between what the giver paid and what the recipient would have paid. Waldfogel found presents from distant givers, such as far-flung grandparents, tend to be the most wasteful.

prompt: Van Baardwijk and Franses found that hemlines move at the same time as the economy, so skirt lengths can warn of a recession.
explanation: They found the economy leads the hemline by about three years, and no effect in the other direction. That lag explains why skirts were short during the 2008 to 2009 recession.

prompt: The habit of focusing on the leftmost digits of a number, which makes $4.99 feel much cheaper than $5.00, is called __________ bias.
explanation: It shows up even in big purchases: used cars lose value in a jump each time the odometer's first digit ticks over.

prompt: In Sarah Hill and colleagues' experiments, what did reminders of a recession do to women's desire for beauty products?
options: Raised it, while desire for most other products fell
Lowered it, along with everything else
Had no effect at all
Raised desire for every kind of product equally
correctAnswer: Raised it, while desire for most other products fell
explanation: The study was the first experimental demonstration of the lipstick effect. Real sales data are messier: in the years before 2008 lipstick sales were weak while lip gloss boomed.

prompt: Match each idea to what it describes:

pairs.right: The gap between a gift's price and its value to the recipient
The folk idea that skirt lengths track the economy
Leonard Lauder's theory that small luxuries sell better in downturns
Why a car at 79,900 miles fetches more than one at 80,000

explanation: All four are about how people value things in ways a simple price tag misses, from sentiment to the first digit on a sticker.
